Three, and nothing else. The drafter records which one it chose (9.3).

## What, why, how

State what happened. Explain why it happened. Show how the reader could apply it. The most
versatile of the three and the right default when nothing else obviously fits.

## Problem, agitate, solve

Name a problem the reader recognises, make them feel what it costs, then show what fixed it. For
posts about a mistake, a frustration or something broken.

## Hook, frame, insight, lesson

The frame is the extra step: name what most people believe before delivering what he found instead.
For posts that challenge an assumption rather than teach a method.

**Josh — this one contradicts your banned-phrases list, and we have left both in place rather than
resolve it quietly.** That list calls "Most people think X..." the single most recognisable AI
cadence on LinkedIn and tells the drafter to delete the rejected half and state the point once. This
framework asks for that construction by name. A drafter reading both is being told to do a thing and
not to do it, and that is the kind of silent conflict that produces a draft nobody can explain.

Our reading is that the framework is sound when the belief being named is one you have actually
heard somebody say, and the ban is right when the belief is a strawman invented to be knocked down.
But that distinction is yours to draw, not ours.

From 134 posts by all eight writers, 14 October 2026. Structure only; none of their words are here.

then lean", and at sentence level this corpus does not do it — the variation is *within* a stretch
rather than between the start, middle and end. Either the rule is about paragraph size rather than
sentence length, or it is your preference rather than something observed. Say which and it gets

# Banned phrases and AI tells

STARTER — written by Thought Pilot, then rebuilt against a detection library. Josh: cut anything you
disagree with, add anything that makes you wince. This is the list the gate checks every draft
against, and the list the writer is handed before drafting.

Three things check it: `measure_draft` flags the loudest ones for free before anything is spent,
`scrub_draft` runs every rule line by line, and gate check 8 judges the finished post against this
text. They read this section, so a change here changes all three.

## The one that matters most

**Never reject a frame in order to assert another one.**

  "It's not X, it's Y." / "This isn't X. This is Y." / "Not because X, but because Y."
  "Most teams do X. The best do Y." / "Forget X. Start Y." / "Less X, more Y."
  "Is it X? No. It's Y." / "Most people think X..." / "At first glance X..." / "Sure, X. But Y."

This is the single most recognisable AI cadence on LinkedIn, and it survives being disguised — the
softened forms above do the same work three sentences later and are the ones that get through.

It is rhetorically empty. It announces a reframe instead of making a point. Real writers state Y.

**The fix is not to reword it. Delete the rejected half entirely and state Y once, with a detail
attached.** "It's not about the tools, it's about the people" becomes "She wanted to know who owned
the number after we left."

**The exception, and the only one: an assumption with an owner.** "The CFO told me the number was
fine" names a belief and challenges it, and it is a scene, because a person held it. What stays
banned is the ownerless version — "most people think", "everyone believes", "the common view is" —
and every softened form of it. The test is not the wording. It is whether a reader could ask who
believed this and get an answer from the post.

Josh asked for this on 19 October: he wants to keep challenging an assumption up front and not the
phrasing that does it. Worth knowing while you apply it: a consensus opening is the rarest shape in
the whole reference corpus, 5 posts in 156, so attributing the belief is not a loophole to lean on.
It is the difference between a scene and a cadence.

## Constructions that give it away

- Throat-clearing: "Here's the thing:" / "Here's what I learned:" / "The truth is," / "Let me be
  clear:" / "It turns out" / "Can we talk about"
- Formulaic reveal: "Let me explain." / "Here's why." / "Here's what happened." Just say it.
- Unearned profundity: "Something shifted." / "Everything changed." / "That was the moment." /
  "Let that sink in." / "Read that again." Delete, unless the line before it earned the weight with
  a specific fact.
- Vague attribution: "Experts argue" / "Studies show" / "Industry reports suggest" / "The data
  tells us". Name the source or cut the claim.
- Copulative avoidance: "serves as", "stands as", "marks a", "represents a", "boasts a",
  "features a", "offers a", "plays a role in", "helps to", "aims to", "seeks to". Use "is" and
  "has". Real writing uses "is" freely; dodging it is a tell.
- Participle traps: "highlighting its importance", "underscoring significance", "paving the way
  for", "reflecting the broader trend", "marking a new era", "signalling a shift". These give the
  rhythm of insight with no claim inside. Name the actual consequence instead.
- Puffery: "a pivotal moment", "a major shift", "broader implications", "a watershed moment", "a
  turning point". When every fact is pivotal, none of it lands.
- False ranges: "from startups to enterprises", "from boardrooms to break rooms". A real range
  narrows a claim; these span everything and say nothing.
- Correlative crutches: "not only... but also", "on one hand... on the other".
- Meta-commentary: "Hint:", "Plot twist:", "Spoiler:", "But that's another post", "In this post".
- Knowledge-cutoff disclaimers: "as of my last update", "based on available information". No human
  writes these.
- Elegant variation: renaming the same company across four sentences — "Acme" then "the agency"
  then "the team" then "the business". Pick one name and repeat it. Pronouns are fine.
- False agency: "complaints become fixes", "the decision emerged", "the strategy evolved". An
  abstract noun performing a human action is how the person gets removed from the sentence. Name
  who did it.
- Narrator distance: "Teams across the industry are realising..." He is not standing above the
  industry watching it. "I watched three teams do the same thing this month" is the same claim from
  inside the room.

## Vocabulary

Verbs: leverage, utilise, delve, harness, navigate, embrace, elevate, unlock, cultivate, foster,
streamline, underscore, embark, empower, facilitate, revolutionise, reimagine, supercharge.

Adjectives: groundbreaking, revolutionary, transformative, cutting-edge, robust, scalable, pivotal,
seamless, comprehensive, innovative, meticulous, profound, dynamic, holistic, disruptive,
unprecedented.

Nouns as metaphor: landscape, realm, tapestry, synergy, testament, paradigm, ecosystem, catalyst,
cornerstone, deep dive, key takeaways, actionable insights, best practices.

Phrases: in today's landscape, in a world where, at the end of the day, at its core, when it comes
to, the reality is, make no mistake, full stop, in conclusion, circle back, move the needle, think
outside the box, let's dive in, let's unpack, game-changer, double down.

Filler: actually, basically, essentially, literally, simply, really, truly, honestly, obviously,
clearly, certainly, definitely, ultimately, fundamentally, absolutely, indeed, furthermore,
moreover, additionally, consequently. Test: delete the word. If the meaning is identical, leave it
deleted.

## Shape and rhythm

- No em dashes. His count across 11,022 words of recorded speech is zero.
- No semicolons. They read as edited prose rather than speech.
- No rule of three. "Simple, practical and powerful" is a rhythm, not three ideas. Pick one.
- No paired adjectives. Pick the stronger one.
- Vary sentence length. A block of 15-25 word sentences with no variance is the strongest
  statistical signal of generated text. Short next to long is the fix.
- Vary paragraph length. Every paragraph the same size is a layout, not writing.
- No repeated bullet shapes. Three bullets opening on the same word, running to the same length, or
  landing on the same grammatical beat read as generated. Real lists are uneven.
- Title case headers are deck formatting. Sentence case.
- No more than one bolded phrase per section.
- Never open with a question. Never open with "I".
- Never end by asking for engagement ("Agree?", "Thoughts?", "What would you add?").
- Never end by restating the post. The last line pushes forward.
- No hashtags.
- Every post needs an edge — a limit, a tradeoff, a place he was wrong. All-positive reads as
  generated even when every rule above passes.
- Use contractions. Too-clean grammar is its own tell.

## NOT banned — and why

These look like violations of the rules above and are not. Each is measured in his own speech, so
removing it would remove him from the post. Do not "fix" these.

- **potentially**, **might** — signature terms in the voiceprint, measured across 11,022 words.
  The hedge rule does not apply to them. Test a hedge properly: remove it, and if the claim now
  overstates the case, the hedge was doing work. Only cut hedges that soften tone without narrowing
  a claim.
- **guys** — how he addresses a room. Not filler.
- **appreciate** — his word, not corporate warmth.
- Deliberate short sentences stacked for rhythm. Three short sentences in a row is a device. The
  uniform-length rule targets a block of mid-length sentences with no variance, which is a
  different thing.
- Sentence fragments, where they carry the beat.

## The test underneath all of it

If a sentence could survive unchanged in someone else's post, cut it or make it specific. Every rule
above is a way of failing that test mechanically, which is the only reason they are written down.

- Allowed, Josh 13 Oct 2026: "here's my very simple system:" (or "here's my system:") as a colon lead-in to a numbered list. His words: "I actually like ... my very simple system". This is a narrow carve-out. "Here's why.", "Here's what happened.", "Here's the thing:" and "Here's what I learned:" stay banned.  _(added 2026-10-13)_

- Extends the 13 Oct carve-out, Josh 13 Oct 2026: "here's my system:" (or "here's my very simple system:") is allowed before any list, numbered or bulleted. Bullets are often needed because the claim check reads list numerals as numbers he never said. "Here's why.", "Here's what happened.", "Here's the thing:" and "Here's what I learned:" stay banned.  _(added 2026-10-13)_

softened forms above do the same work three sentences later and are the ones that get through.

It is rhetorically empty. It announces a reframe instead of making a point. Real writers state Y.

attached.** "It's not about the tools, it's about the people" becomes "She wanted to know who owned

**59 posts across 7 accounts were collected on 7 September 2026 and measured. Their words are not
here and never will be.**

The posts live in the scraping console, which is their store of record. This section holds only
what came out of the measurement: counts, medians and categories. That is not a policy someone
has to remember — the derivation script refuses to emit anything containing a run of the source
text, so a draft cannot quote what this system does not hold.

---

## The finding that matters most

**Almost nobody opens with a question. 147 of 1899 posts do.**

Josh's hook rule — a question may close a hook, never start one — is not a stylistic
preference. It is what 92% of the writers he chose already do.

Two more that corroborate his own rules:

- **63 of 1899 posts ask for engagement.**
- **228 of 1899 carry a direct ask** — about 1 in 8.

## Per account

| Account | Posts | Median words | Above fold | Paragraphs | Lists | Variation |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Adam Treboutat | 250 | 313.5 | 20 | 13 | 80% | 10.9 |
| Aman Ghataura | 250 | 142 | 23 | 10 | 75% | 10.6 |
| Curtis Howland | 250 | 275 | 21 | 13 | 82% | 13.9 |
| Jen Allen-Knuth | 249 | 193 | 63 | 9 | 24% | 7.1 |
| Julia Carter | 250 | 181.5 | 55.5 | 8 | 40% | 18.8 |
| Matt Barker | 250 | 183.5 | 39 | 13 | 65% | 9.3 |
| 🦾Eric Nowoslawski | 250 | 256.5 | 66 | 12 | 46% | 9.7 |
| Ryan Carlin | 150 | 401.5 | 23 | 21 | 63% | 14.9 |

_Measured 2026-10-20 across 8 accounts and 1899 posts. Their words are not stored anywhere in this system._

<!-- sentinel-measurements:end -->

Josh asked to lean most into Matt Barker — his frameworks, structures and methods, in Josh's
voice. This is what his posts DO, structurally. None of his words are here and none may reach a
draft (8.3). Two numbers to read it against, both from the measurements above:

- **250 posts**, 2026-03-02 to 2026-10-19, median **183.5 words** — the third shortest of the 8.
- Sentence-length variation **9.3** — the second most uniform of the 8. He writes in steadier lengths than his reputation for punchiness suggests.

eight whose commonest opening is anything other than a plain statement, and the nearest any of
the other seven gets to his rate is 27%. If one move is worth taking from him, it is this one.

detail does the work a credential would otherwise do.

the person it happened to.** That is a reading of his openings rather than a measurement, and it
is offered as one. It matters for Josh because a shape built around someone else's situation
survives anonymising, where one built around a named account does not.

Matt's version puts somebody else at the centre. For Josh that is the easier version to write
honestly, because his material is client work he cannot name.

version of this read called his opening *a scene, not a cut*, on eight posts that put him at
61.5. At 241 he is at 39, and the opposite is true: he gets in fast and explains afterwards.

(**72%**) against 44% across the corpus, and his median turn lands **0.16** of the way through
against 0.25. He sets up and reverses inside the first few sentences and spends the rest on the
consequence. Measured sentence-wise by `scripts/measure-structure.mjs` on 20 October, so it does
not depend on a line break surviving.

from the line breaks rather than inferred. That is above the corpus and below Curtis Howland's
82%. The pattern underneath the number is a judgement, not a count: numbered steps when the
point IS a process, unbroken prose when the point is a judgement.

is for. It does the altitude filtering Josh's hook section asks of the opening, except Matt does
it again in the middle, where a reader who has stayed is deciding whether this is for them.
Directly transferable, and nothing in Josh's rules covers it.

from-to, a share, a count) and attributed to the person it happened to. It reads as reporting.

## How he lands

**Short.** 99 of 241 posts end in eight words or fewer (**41%**), the highest of the eight.

passes 4%. It is the most distinctive thing about his endings and nothing in Josh's rules
mentions it.

Said plainly, because it is the most recognisable thing he does and the reason a draft that
imitates him fails Josh's own gate.

**His turn renames the reader's problem.** The structure is: state the problem the reader
thinks they have, deny it, substitute a renamed one. That is exactly the construction the
banned-phrases section forbids — rejecting a frame in order to assert another — and it is the

problem is one he can evidence. The system still must not copy it. The fix is the one already in
that section: delete the rejected half and state the second problem once, with the detail
attached.

nothing here detects a renamed problem mechanically. Given the closing claim beside it turned
out backwards on six posts, treat this as the judgement it is until something measures it.

**This section said he did, and that was wrong.** It was written off six posts collected on
5 October whose line breaks the scrape had stripped, so they were read by eye. Counted across
**241** posts he closes on an ask — direct or engagement — **22 times**, which is **9%**.

five, which is 20%. So Matt asks less often than the other seven, and less often than Josh's
rule allows. He is the most restrained closer of the eight, not the outlier.

have 241. **Nothing about his closing needs to be ruled out for Josh.** The rule that rations a
direct ask stays, because it is Josh's rule and it was never Matt's to justify — but it is no
longer a place where leaning into Matt would breach it.

1. **Open on a number.** Half his posts do (**50%**), and he is the only one of the eight who
   leads with one. The strongest-evidenced move here by a distance.
2. **Turn early.** His median turn is at 0.16 against the corpus 0.25, and he turns in 72% of
   posts against 44%. The turn buys the rest of the post; it is not the climax.
3. **Get in fast — 39 words above the fold**, second fewest of the eight. Explain afterwards.
4. **Anchor it to something mundane and specific.** A weekday and an errand beat an adjective.
5. **Land short** — 41% of his closes are eight words or fewer, the highest here.
6. **One mechanism per post.** List it only if it is genuinely a process.
7. **Name the audience once, in the middle.** New to Josh's rules, and cheap.

Not: the renamed-problem turn. That is the only one, and it is a judgement rather than a count.

**Josh — this is a real fork.** We have kept your banned-phrases rule and ruled Matt's turn out
of bounds, because an over-strict gate fails visibly and is easy to correct. If you want that
construction available because it is how he lands a post, say so and it comes out of the banned
list — but it would then be allowed everywhere, and it is the one pattern most likely to make a
draft read as generated.

_Counted across 250 posts, 2026-03-02 to 2026-10-19. Shape figures rest on the 241 that kept
their line breaks. The previous version of this section rested on six posts and got his closing
habit backwards; the numbers above are what replaced it._

---

Their words, their cadence, their phrasing. Not quoted, not near-quoted, not paraphrased. If a run
of words from one of these could be recognised in a draft, it has been used wrongly. Josh's voice
comes from the voice guide and nowhere else.

**One specific caution, Josh.** Matt Barker is not a peer reference here — he is the origin of your
rules. His 3 September post states the lived-experience test, "lessons not advice", and the
frame-then-reveal structure in almost the words you sent us. That makes his cadence the single most
likely to leak into a draft, because the system is already aligned to his thinking. Take his
structure knowingly, and be suspicious of any draft that starts to sound like him.

  statistical signal of generated text. Short next to long is the fix.
- Vary paragraph length. Every paragraph the same size is a layout, not writing.
- No repeated bullet shapes. Three bullets opening on the same word, running to the same length, or
  landing on the same grammatical beat read as generated. Real lists are uneven.
- Title case headers are deck formatting. Sentence case.
- No more than one bolded phrase per section.
- Never open with a question. Never open with "I".
- Never end by asking for generic engagement ("Agree?", "Thoughts?", "What would you add?") — a question anyone could answer, asked to farm replies. A GENUINE question is not this: the closes section calls it the default close, and it stays allowed. The test is whether only your reader could answer it.
- Never end by restating the post. The last line pushes forward.
- No hashtags.
- Every post needs an edge — a limit, a tradeoff, a place he was wrong. All-positive reads as
  generated even when every rule above passes.
- Use contractions. Too-clean grammar is its own tell.

## NOT banned — and why

These look like violations of the rules above and are not. Each is measured in his own speech, so
removing it would remove him from the post. Do not "fix" these.

- **potentially**, **might** — signature terms in the voiceprint, measured across 11,022 words.
  The hedge rule does not apply to them. Test a hedge properly: remove it, and if the claim now
  overstates the case, the hedge was doing work. Only cut hedges that soften tone without narrowing
  a claim.
- **guys** — how he addresses a room. Not filler.
- **appreciate** — his word, not corporate warmth.
- Deliberate short sentences stacked for rhythm. Three short sentences in a row is a device. The
  uniform-length rule targets a block of mid-length sentences with no variance, which is a
  different thing.
- Sentence fragments, where they carry the beat.

## The test underneath all of it

If a sentence could survive unchanged in someone else's post, cut it or make it specific. Every rule
above is a way of failing that test mechanically, which is the only reason they are written down.

- Allowed, Josh 13 Oct 2026: "here's my very simple system:" (or "here's my system:") as a colon lead-in to a numbered list. His words: "I actually like ... my very simple system". This is a narrow carve-out. "Here's why.", "Here's what happened.", "Here's the thing:" and "Here's what I learned:" stay banned.  _(added 2026-10-13)_

- Extends the 13 Oct carve-out, Josh 13 Oct 2026: "here's my system:" (or "here's my very simple system:") is allowed before any list, numbered or bulleted. Bullets are often needed because the claim check reads list numerals as numbers he never said. "Here's why.", "Here's what happened.", "Here's the thing:" and "Here's what I learned:" stay banned.  _(added 2026-10-13)_

# Who he is talking to

A more sophisticated reader than most advice assumes.

Nearly all LinkedIn writing advice is built for solo operators, freelancers and early-stage
founders. Josh's buyer is not that, and this is the single biggest adjustment the system makes.
Every other rule sits underneath this one.

- **The person.** A VP of Business Development, a VP of Sales, or a head of inside sales. That level.
- **The company.** A vertical SaaS business, Series A through Series C.
- **The motion.** An existing outbound motion. Nobody is starting from zero.
- **The team.** At least five SDRs, BDRs or account executives doing the outreach.
- **Who they sell to.** SMB and mid-market.
- **The pain.** Not booking the meetings they want. Volume is not the problem. Quality and
  prioritisation are.

## Two words that get misread

**Sophisticated** means their operating vocabulary at the altitude they work at. The writing stays
plain, and jargon still fails.

**Strategic** means altitude, not vagueness. A strategic post still carries a specific number, a
specific person and a specific Tuesday. A post for this buyer talks about how a segment gets
chosen. A post for a beginner talks about which button to press.

## The reader who never engages

Josh's buyer lurks. They read and do not like, comment or repost. Do not write for the reader who
reacts; write for the one who reads it and says nothing.

- Write for a sophisticated reader, not a technical one. Write about their decisions, not the mechanics of the build. Josh, 21 Oct 2026.  _(added 2026-10-21)_

- Plain words. No term a reader outside the build wouldn't follow ("calling", "who makes the call" and "a risk named in an audit plan" all failed). The advice has to hold for any reader, not just Josh's own build, one client, one industry or one country. Josh, 21 Oct 2026.  _(added 2026-10-21)_

- The findings, not the method. This reader does not want the dataset, how the data was gathered, or what looked wrong in it — they want what was found and what it means for them. "No one cares about that. This audience doesn't care about that. What they care about is the findings and what it means for them." Josh, 27 Oct 2026.  _(added 2026-10-27)_
